blocks.heading: Classifying communication
blocks.text: Internal communication takes place within the business; external communication crosses its boundary to customers, suppliers or other outside parties. One-way communication sends information without a response as part of that exchange; two-way communication includes feedback between sender and receiver. These distinctions describe different features and can be combined. An internal staff discussion is internal and two-way; a supplier conversation is external and two-way; a notice to staff can be internal and one-way. Written does not automatically mean one-way, since an email exchange can include replies, and speaking is not automatically two-way if no response is allowed. Identify the parties and the opportunity for feedback instead of assuming the medium settles every classification.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nali Goods posts a staff notice that allows no replies, then its manager phones a supplier and discusses a delayed delivery. The notice is internal and one-way. The supplier discussion is external and two-way. The classifications depend on the business boundary and feedback, not whether one channel is electronic.

blocks.heading: Internal communication
blocks.text: Internal communication is communication between people or groups within the same business. It can move downward as instructions, upward as reports or horizontally between departments. The direction does not change its internal boundary. Suitable internal communication helps staff coordinate and raise problems before commitments are missed.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Kira Stores’ sales team asks its warehouse team whether a product is available. Both teams are inside Kira, so the exchange is internal. A later reply to a customer would be external.

blocks.heading: External communication
blocks.text: External communication is communication between a business and parties outside it, such as suppliers, customers, lenders or government bodies. It can inform, negotiate, request or respond. Confidentiality and accuracy matter because misleading information can damage relationships or decisions. Electronic contact can be either internal or external; identify the participants.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Nura Print asks its paper supplier to confirm a delivery date. The supplier is outside Nura’s organisation, so the exchange is external even if the two firms work closely together.

blocks.heading: One-way communication
blocks.text: One-way communication transmits a message without a return response as part of that communication. A notice or announcement can deliver consistent information quickly to many people, but the sender cannot immediately use questions to check understanding. It may suit simple information, while complex or disputed changes often need an opportunity for feedback.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Hila Goods posts a closing-date announcement and offers no response channel in that notice. The notice is one-way in the described exchange. A later discussion would be a separate feedback opportunity rather than proof the original notice checked understanding.

blocks.heading: Two-way communication
blocks.text: Two-way communication includes feedback or exchange between sender and receiver. Questions, replies and clarification can expose misunderstandings and improve decisions. It may take more time than a simple announcement, and it works only if people can respond meaningfully. It need not be face to face: a written exchange can also be two-way.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Foods’ manager emails a proposed rota and staff reply with questions that the manager answers. The written exchange is two-way because responses and clarification are included. Written does not automatically mean one-way.
